newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Cash hungry Russia to build muni junk bond market.
newsitem.headline: Cash hungry Russia to build muni junk bond market.

text.p: Russia plans to turn its junk debt into junk bonds and build a new market for capital-hungry regional issuers in the process, the Finance Ministry said on Monday.

"If everything succeeds as we plan, this will be an undoubted breakthrough for regional-municipal securities," Finance Ministry securities department deputy director Marina Chekurova told a news conference.

Russia plans to convert massive unrepaid 1996 federal agricultural credits into regional bonds which will be auctioned and traded from June 19 on the Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX), Chekurova said.

The Russian treasury will reap a few trillion roubles from the unpaid agro-credits in its newest effort to collect unpaid debts and taxes that have forced Russia to cut 1997 budget spending to less than 70 percent of plan through April.
But backwards regions from Europe to Siberian Yakutia, without the credit-worthiness or sophistication to issue paper on international markets. will get important training.
"There is no civilised market," Chekurova said.

If the new market is a success, the few existing regional and municipal bond issuers could also move to MICEX, according to rules similar to those of the federal Treasury bill market which has successfully attracted foreign investors.
"If they see that the market is more transparent, they can get more money from this market, they can transform their former issues into these new issues," Chekurova said.

The nominal value of the new market will be about nine trillion roubles ($2.6 billion) in the form of about 210 different securities backed by over 70 regions, securities department director Bella Zlatkis said last week.
Chekurova said the market could grow by another trillion roubles next year if some established regions made new issues.

St Petersburg, the largest muni issuer, has several trillion roubles nominal outstanding, while the federal government typically issues 12 trillion roubles of paper a week, and T-bill daily trading volume can be around six trillion roubles.

Deputy Finance Minister Vasily Kovalyov, who heads a working group on the regional bond project, said another five trillion roubles in credits deferred until 1998 would be converted if not paid in the mean time.
Regions which flatly refused to work out a way to pay up would would face financial sanctions within a month, he said.
"Any normal head of a region knows a simple fact -- you have to pay your debts," Kovalyov said, using a logic Russia is forcing on its debtors regularly.

Russia's biggest carmaker AvtoVAZ will restructure its tax debt by issuing a controlling stake of new shares in the company to the government, which the government can sell if VAZ falls behind in arrears payments.
And one of its biggest oil companies Yuganskneftegaz is using an alternative scheme to issue asset-backed securities to the government while it pays off its tax debts.
Kovalyov said Russia was forced into action by the failure of past policies. "We need the money now," he said.
